stops.name: Curzola, captured in the sea-fight
stops.campa: Venice and Genoa are at open war again, and Marco, three years home, restless, perhaps commanding a galley of his own, sails with the Venetian fleet that meets the Genoese under Lamba Doria off the island of Curzola in the Adriatic. The battle goes hard against Venice: dozens of galleys sunk or taken, thousands of Venetians dead or captured, Marco among the prisoners marched off to Genoa in chains. It is the single worst defeat the Republic suffers in the long Genoese wars, and it delivers into Genoese hands, by the accident of one lost sea-fight, the one Venetian whose testimony will outlast every doge of his century.

stops.name: Genoa: the prison, Rustichello, the book dictated
stops.campa: Held through the winter in the prison of the Palazzo di San Giorgio, Marco shares his cell with Rustichello of Pisa, a professional writer of romances taken prisoner on the war's other front, who recognizes in the Venetian's endless talk of Cathay and Cipangu and the Great Khan's court the richest unwritten book in Italy. Through the winter of 1298 into 1299 Marco dictates and Rustichello shapes it into Franco-Italian prose, part travel-report, part chivalric romance, until the manuscript called Il Milione, the Book of the Marvels of the World, exists: the ransom, in the end, that buys Marco lasting fame if not his liberty.
stops.quote: Since our Lord God did mould with his hands our first Father Adam, even until this day, never hath there been Christian, or Pagan, or Tartar, or Indian, or any man of any nation, who in his own person hath had so much knowledge and experience of the divers parts of the World and its Wonders as hath had this Messer Marco!
stops.quote_source: Il Milione / The Travels of Marco Polo, Prologue (Yule-Cordier translation)

stops.name: Venice, freed by the Peace of Milan
stops.campa: The Peace of Milan ends the Venetian-Genoese war in the summer of 1299 and releases the prisoners of Curzola on both sides; Marco comes home to the Corte del Milione a second time, already half-famous, for copies of the Genoa manuscript begin circulating in Italian, Latin, and Franco-Venetian within a few years, read as much for marvel as for fact. Venetians who cannot credit his numbers (a hundred thousand of this, a million of that) nickname him, half affectionately, Marco Milioni, and the courtyard where his family lives takes the name that survives to this day: Corte del Milion.

stops.name: Venice, marriage to Donata Badoer
stops.campa: Past forty-five, Marco marries Donata, daughter of the merchant Vitale Badoer, and the household in the Corte del Milione fills with the ordinary weather of Venetian domestic life after a quarter-century of desert and court: three daughters born in turn, Fantina, Bellela, and Moreta, none of whom will ever cross the sea their father crossed twice over. He resumes trade as a Venetian merchant of standing, invests in galleys and partnerships, sits on no great office, and is remembered by neighbors chiefly as a comfortable, talkative man who will not stop telling the same impossible stories about Cathay to anyone who will listen.

stops.name: Venice, the merchant decades, and the doubters at the door
stops.campa: For two more decades Marco lives the unremarkable life of a Venetian man of business: lawsuits over a runaway slave, a partnership settling his uncle Maffeo's estate, small quarrels over inheritance with a cousin, while his book, copied and re-copied, spreads through the courts and countinghouses of Europe and gathers both fame and open scorn together. Visitors come to his door specifically to scoff at his numbers; the doubt follows him toward the grave and past it, so that within a decade of his death the chronicler Jacopo d'Acqui will already be setting down the deathbed scene as a settled piece of Venetian legend.

stops.name: Venice, the will and the death
stops.campa: Ill and confined to his house, Marco dictates his last testament on the eighth of January, freeing a Tartar servant named Peter he had brought back from Cathay and leaving his estate to Donata and his three daughters; he dies within a day, on the eighth or ninth of January 1324, and is buried, tradition says, at the church of San Lorenzo, his grave later lost when the church was rebuilt. The legend that outlives the parchment has him ringed at the last by friends and a friar begging him to unsay his marvels and die shriven of exaggeration, and Marco refusing to the end: he has not told even half of what he saw.
stops.quote: I have not told half of what I saw, for I knew I would not be believed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by tradition to Jacopo d'Acqui, Imago Mundi seu Chronica (c. 1330), the earliest recorded version of the deathbed legend
